column1: Does static imply inline for class members?
column2:
No. A static data member is shared by instances; static alone does not make its definition inline. Since C++17, inline static allows a definition in a shared header. A static constexpr data member is implicitly inline since C++17.

class Counter {
public:
    static int created;          // declaration; not inline
    inline static int total = 0; // inline definition, C++17
};

column1: Which member functions are implicitly inline when defined inside a class?
column2:
In ordinary header-based code, functions defined inside the class are implicitly inline, including static member functions. This allows matching definitions in multiple translation units under the ODR rules; it does not guarantee machine-code inlining. Merely being a member does not give an out-of-class definition this property.

// counter.hpp
class Counter {
public:
    int Value() const { return value_; } // implicitly inline
    static int Zero() { return 0; }     // implicitly inline
private:
    int value_ = 0;
};

column1: How can an ordinary mutable static data member be declared and defined across files?
column2:
Declare it inside the class in the header and define it once in a .cpp file. Since C++17, inline static permits the definition and initializer directly inside the class, with no separate .cpp definition. The member remains one shared object.

// counter.hpp
class Counter { public: static int created; };

// counter.cpp
#include "counter.hpp"
int Counter::created = 0;

// Alternative since C++17, in the header:
// class Counter { public: inline static int created = 0; };

column1: Is a pointer an integer because its value represents an address?
column2:
No. A pointer has its own type, such as int* or Widget*, not int or size_t. An address can be displayed numerically, but this does not change the pointer type. Typed pointers support operations based on the pointed-to type; a pointer type alone does not guarantee a live object at that address.

int value = 7;
int* p = &value; // p has type int*
std::cout << static_cast<const void*>(p); // displays an address
// A one-past pointer also has type int*,
// but it must not be dereferenced.
